title: Array Reversal: Two Pointers, One Pass
oneLiner: Walk from both ends at once, swapping as the pointers close in.
keyTakeaway: Two pointers starting at opposite ends and walking inward is the standard way to do array work in O(1) extra space, instead of allocating a second array.
explanation: First taste of a technique with its own name: two pointers moving toward each other. Instead of one index walking left to right, use two -- one starting at the front, one at the back -- and swap-and-step-inward until they meet or cross. This is the earliest, simplest version of the "two pointers" pattern you'll see formalized later in the Patterns track. Watch out for the stopping condition: `left < right`, not `left <= right` -- with `<=` on an odd-length array you'd swap the middle element with itself and (harmlessly here, but it's the same bug class as an infinite loop elsewhere) waste a step.

visualizationSteps.message: left starts at index 0, right starts at the last index. Swap them, then step both pointers inward.
Step inward: left -> 1, right -> 4. Still left < right, so keep swapping.
Step inward: left -> 2, right -> 3. Still left < right, so keep swapping.
Pointers crossed. Done -- the whole array is reversed in place, no extra array needed.

complexity.note: n/2 swaps between two pointers; nothing allocated -- 'in place' is exactly the O(1) space claim.

referenceSolutions.python:
def reverse_array(nums):
    left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while left < right:
        nums[left], nums[right] = nums[right], nums[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return nums
